sections.title: Why put a queue in the middle

blocks.text: A message queue decouples a producer from a consumer in time and in capacity. The producer hands off work and returns immediately; consumers process at their own pace. This absorbs traffic spikes (the queue fills, workers catch up), isolates failures (a slow email provider doesn't slow checkout), and lets you add new consumers without changing producers.

cols.title: Message queue (SQS, RabbitMQ)
pros: Each message delivered to one consumer, then deleted

cols.title: Distributed log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar)
pros: Messages retained for days; many consumer groups read independently
cons: Consumer tracks offsets; per-message retry is awkward

blocks.caption: Topic with 3 partitions, replicated across brokers

items: A **topic** is split into **partitions**; each partition is an append-only log with sequential **offsets**.
Producers choose the partition by hashing the message key — all events for one key (an order, a user) land in one partition, **in order**.
Each partition has a leader and followers (replication factor 3). `acks=all` waits for the in-sync replicas.
A **consumer group** shares partitions among its members: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group. Different groups read the same data independently.
Consumers commit offsets; after a crash, a consumer resumes from the last committed offset.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Assume at-least-once and make consumers idempotent: upsert by a natural key, or record processed message ids.

items: Order is guaranteed only **within a partition**. Choose the key so that events needing order share it.
Consumers in a group ≤ partitions; extra consumers sit idle. Plan partitions for peak parallelism (you can add partitions later, but keys remap).
Hot keys overload one partition — salt the key if strict per-key order isn't required.
Transient failure: retry with backoff; in Kafka, use retry topics with delays (retry-1m, retry-10m) so one bad message doesn't block the partition.
Permanent failure (poison message): send to a **dead-letter queue** with the error, alert, and keep going.
Watch **consumer lag** (latest offset − committed offset) — it's the key health metric; autoscale consumers on it.
Retention lets you replay: fix a bug, reset the group's offsets, reprocess.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: For order events I'd use Kafka keyed by order_id so each order's events stay ordered, with consumers that are idempotent because delivery is at-least-once. For background jobs like sending emails, a simple queue with a DLQ is enough.
